analytic.title: Blocking-Waived Estimation: Improving the Worst-Case End-To-End Delay Analysis in Switched Ethernet

div.p: As time-sensitive networks must guarantee the endto-end delay requirement of data flows, the worst-case delay (WCD) analysis is mandatory. To date, several analytical approaches have been proposed for WCD analysis, mainly in two classes: network-calculus approaches (NC), and real-time scheduling-oriented approaches such as response-time analysis (RTA), and compositional performance analysis (CPA). In spite of advances in WCD analysis techniques, the computation of the exact worst-case delay faces combinatorial explosion issues, therefore several approaches have been developed to provide an upper bound with more or less pessimism. Nevertheless, reducing pessimism remains challenging, and each approach differs from others in specific scenarios. In this context, this paper provides a comprehensive comparative study that analyzes the results of WCD calculation approaches under the Nonpreemptive Fixed Priority Scheduling Policy. To further reduce the pessimism, we propose a new algorithm BWE (Blocking-Waived Estimation) built for switched network architectures upon RTA, which further investigates the relationship between blocking time and transmission time of the flow of interest (e.g., virtual link in AFDX) in adjacent hops. As illustrated in an example network architecture, the result produced by BWE is generally less pessimistic (the WCD is reduced by at maximum 34.34%) compared to the state-of-the-art RTA/CPA calculation results.

div.head: I. INTRODUCTION
div.p: Real-time systems, particularly those distributed on switched Ethernet such as Avionics Full-Duplex Switched Ethernet (AFDX) and Time-Sensitive Networking (TSN), are witnessing a burgeoning demand since they provide predictability and determinism. Within this context, the tight computation of end-to-end worst-case delay (WCD) emerges as a pivotal element. The WCD represents the maximum possible delay that a message or data frame might encounter as it traverses a switched network from source to destination. This metric, WCD, is not merely a theoretical construct but a vital tool for evaluating network performance quality. Since real-time communication in some domains, such as industrial automation, smart grid, automobile and avionics embedded systems is on the basis of the fact that information is transmitted/shared by respecting the timing constraints, the significance of timing be-havior, including WCD, is amplified. Computing WCD upper bound is provides the assurance of timely message delivery in compliance with stringent real-time scheduling demands inherent in Ethernet Network environments but can also lead to over-provisioning of network resources if the bound is not tight with respect to the true WCD. In fact, tighter WCD bound estimation leads to less network bandwidth allocation, allowing thus to admit more application data flows in practice.

To date, the academic and industrial communities have proposed several methodologies to estimate WCD under diverse scenarios, mainly including two basic classes: NC and realtime scheduling theory based [1]. These support both elementary architectural designs and more complex, switch-based network structures [2]. Each methodology is characterized by its unique set of merits and limitations [3]. Given this diversity, a comparative analysis that discerns the nuanced differences among these methodologies is of great importance. Such an analysis is essential for advancing towards more refined and tighter results, particularly for non-preemptive strict priority traffic flows within switched networks.

In this paper, therefore, we undertake an exploration of the multiple extant WCD analysis approaches to conduct a comparative study based on a switched network architecture. We compare network calculus (by using Saihu [4]), Compositional Performance Analysis (CPA) (by using the pyCPA tool [2]), and Response-Time Analysis (RTA) (by using the algorithm of [5]). To reduce the pessimism produced in the above approaches, particularly in RTA, we propose BWE, a novel approach to tighten WCD of frames in the network architecture by avoiding the overlapped calculation between the transmissions of blocking and target frames of adjacent hops that otherwise would lead to over-estimating the WCD bound.

The contribution of the paper is threefold: First, we conduct an analysis to identify the primary reasons behind the pessimism prevalent in the RTA approach and unveil the causes behind the overestimation of WCD in it. Second, we propose BWE, a novel method enhancing RTA by addressing the identified causes of pessimism through a tighter bound for WCD calculations. Lastly, we further validate the effectiveness of BWE through a numerical comparison involving RTA, CPA, and NC on an AFDX use-case [3]. We observe that BWE not only outperforms RTA and CPA but also shows competitive and, in some respects superior performance in comparison to NC.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews the related WCD analysis approaches. Section III describes the properties of real-time data flows in terms of virtual links and their transmission policies of data frames. Our proposed approach, named BWE, is detailed in Section IV. The comparative study between different WCD approaches and a performance evaluation of BWE are presented in Section V. Section VI draws the conclusion and outlines our future work.

div.head: II. RELATED WORK
div.p: The worst-case end-to-end delay analysis is NP-hard [6, Thm 10.2] due to the complex inter-data flow interference and queuing patterns that a flow of interest may experience when traversing multiple shared switches in its path from the source to the destinations (multicast). Numerous approaches have been proposed to switched-Ethernet-based architectures such as AFDX and TSN. They are either based on the networkcalculus theory or the real-time scheduling theory.

In this paper we consider the WCD analysis of sporadic data flows with minimal inter-arrival period, characterized by virtual links like in AFDX (Avionics Full-Duplex) [7], and under Non-preemptive Fixed Priority scheduling policy in Ethernet switches and end nodes. The choice of AFDX is justified by the fact that almost all the existing WCD analysis approaches have been applied to AFDX, providing a common experimental use-case to compare the approaches. Readers interested in the WCD analysis approaches applied to TSN may refer to a collection of references [8]. Furthermore, among the numerous approaches applied to AFDX, we choose to only focus on NC, RTA, and CPA.

Other approaches such as model-checking based [9], Trajectory analysis (from destination node to source) [10] and Forward Analysis (from source to destination) [11] are not included. In general model checking based approaches suffer from the combinatorial explosion issue as flow interference with all possible offsets (i.e., different starting time of flows) must be examined. Trajectory analysis intends to provide tighter WCD bound to reduce the pessimism but could be too optimistic (i.e., underestimate the WCD) in some corner cases [12]. The identified issues have been corrected in [10], but without formal proof, although it has been further revised [13]. Forward Analysis has also been designed for further tightening the WCD bound and is quite promising by explicitly considering the serialization effect on the link [11]. However, a recent work has shown that it also suffers from the optimistic issue, although it has been reduced [14]. As model-checking based approach is hardly scalable, and both Trajectory analysis and Forward Analysis present optimistic issue, they are not further considered in this paper.

Network calculus (NC) [15,6,16] is one of the first approaches proposed for WCD analysis in AFDX. As a branch of network theory, it provides a set of mathematical tools to understand and model the flow of data (such as frames) in a network. It employs min-plus algebra, characterizes the traffic with arrival curves, and defines service guarantees using service curves. Its primary application is in the domain of Quality of Service (QoS) in networks, where it is crucial to ensure that performance metrics like bandwidth, delay, and throughput meet certain predefined standards. The current NCrelated tools include DiscoDNC [17], RTC Toolbox [18], and Saihu (that includes 4 tools for TSN analysis) [4], but they are implemented differently and possess different strengths and weaknesses [4]. Despite the prevalence of NC, the algorithm still faces issues such as frame misordering that could increase the delay in transmission due to frame replication [19].

The class of real-time scheduling approaches encompasses WCD calculation methods such as response time analysis (RTA). RTA was first proposed and used in the field of realtime systems to determine the worst-case response time of tasks in a computing system [5]. It considers the worst-case execution time, task prioritization, blocking times, and preemption impacts of frames sent across the network and calculate their worst-case response time. Built upon the essence of RTA, Compositional Performance Analysis (CPA) incorporates the logic foundations from it [20]. Authors in [21] assessed the WCD in a strict-priority Ethernet network using CPA. CPA focuses on a scheduling analysis of a subpart of the system, the 'component', and drastically reduces the complexity of WCD analysis. However, the reduction in complexity leads to pessimism for the WCD bound.

In spite of their advancements, the approaches discussed above still introduce pessimism into the WCD calculation. In industrial applications, this pessimism may lead to an unacceptable over-provisioning of the network resources. In order to provide a more reliable estimation of the WCD in AFDX systems by reducing pessimism, we scrutinize the RTA methodology and investigate the underlying causes of pessimism. We discover that there lacks prior work into exploring the relationship between the amount of blocking time and transmission time of target data flow of adjacent nodes in RTA. In the context of these findings, we propose BWE, an innovative and more stringent WCD estimation method that distinctively circumvents the redundant calculations appearing in RTA, thereby refining the precision of WCD estimations.

div.head: III. SYSTEM MODEL
div.p: We consider an asynchronous frame-switching network with full-duplex transmission links. The AFDX network architecture contains multiple switches with store-and-forward input ports, end-systems (ES), and virtual links (VL). Each frame is stored in the input port and forwarded to the output port as soon as its last bit is received (store-and-forward).
Each VL is assigned to a priority, typically 0 to 7 in Ethernet, and periodically sends out frames to one (unicast) or several (multicast) destinations with fixed maximum frame sizes.

Without loss of generality, we assume that all links have the same transmission rate and we define the transmission time C j of a virtual link V j as the maximum frame size of the VL, divided by the transmission rate. Hence, C j does not depend on the considered transmission link. We also denote by T j the period of the virtual link V j , i.e., the elapsed time between the emission of two consecutive frames. Frames of VLs are sent from the corresponding ES source to the first intermediate switch and then transmitted from this switch to the destination end-system or to another intermediate switch. We assume that the switches are not overloaded, which we write
div.formula: n j=1 C j T j ≤ 1(1)
div.p: at each output port, where n is the number of VLs traversing the output port. The output ports in the switches use a nonpreemptive fixed priority scheduling policy: When a frame is being transmitted, other frames with higher or equal priorities cannot preempt the current transmission. At each hop, frames can be blocked by other frames with either higher or equal priorities but at most once by a frame with lower priority. The set of VLs transmitting frames is denoted as follows:
div.formula: VL ≜ {V L j } , 1 ≤ j ≤ |VL|(2)
div.p: In the paper, we focus on a VL of interest (target VL), which we denote by V L i . We denote by LP i , EP i , HP i , the sets of virtual links with respectively lower, equal or higher priority than the virtual link of interest V L i . Table I contains the list of notations for the paper.

div.head: IV. BWE: BLOCKING-WAIVED ESTIMATION
div.p: This section first gives an overview of response-time analysis (RTA) and then analyzes its limitations. Next, we introduce Blocking-Waived Estimation (BWE), a novel approach for addressing the overestimation produced by the original RTA method.

A. Overview of Response-Time Analysis (RTA) RTA is commonly used for a tight recursive WCD calculation of V L i . The stability constraint of Equation ( 1) ensures the convergence of the RTA algorithm. It involves studying the response time that blocks the transmission of V L i for each hop. In RTA, end-to-end WCD is calculated by the summation of response time on each hop based on VL's priorities and the transmission time of V L i . More specifically, the response time in each hop k is computed by the recursive Equation (3) involving the maximum transmission time of frames in LP i and sum of blocking time from EP i and HP i , with I k ′ i initialized as 0 [22,23]:

div.p: the blocking amount due to frames from virtual links from higher or equal priorities; and I k ′ i is referred as blocking time (also called interference), which is computed recursively with the fixed point recurrence. As the recurrence value I k ′ i is initialized with 0 (could also be any other value smaller than the worst-case blocking time, if we look for accelerating the convergence in practice) and computed recursively until it converges. If the convergence condition of Equation (1) holds, then I k ′ i converges to a fixed point (i.e., I k ′ i from previous iteration is equal to I k ′ i in the current iteration from Equation ( 3)). In this case, I k ′ i is assigned to I k i . The worstcase delay of the k th hop w k i is calculated as:

div.p: The worst-case delay for a k th hop w k i is the addition of the transmission time of target virtual link V L i and the blocking time from the hop. Since we consider a frameswitching system with multiple ES (End System) and switches, frames from each target VL V L i will travel through several transmission hops (at least two in our case). The end-to-end WCD W i should be the summation of the WCD in each hop:
div.formula: W i = k w k i (6)
div.p: RTA aims to provide an algorithm with low pessimism in the network systems by calculating an accurate estimation of the worst-case response time of frame transmission. As RTA employs recursive refinement to improve the accuracy of response time estimates, the analysis is repeated until a stable response time is achieved (I k i = I k ′ i ). This recursive process allows for adjustments on WCD calculation after checking the convergence condition, leading to reduced pessimism.

The RTA algorithm is described in Algorithm 1. It first selects the maximum blocking time among frames with lower priorities than the frame from target V L i , as shown in Line 4. By considering the blocking time from priority and scheduling policies, the algorithm demonstrates the recursive nature of RTA with the loop from Line 6 to Line 10, where the WCD for each transmission hop is calculated and accumulated until frames from a specific VL reach their destination. When applied to real-time systems, to ensure obtaining right WCD, the Algorithm 1 is repeated for busy periods until r + 2LCM , where r is the release time of the first frame of V L i and LCM is the Least Common Multiple of all periods of active ES sources [24], [23].

RTA Limitation
div.p: However, the RTA approach overestimates the worst-case delay by repeatedly adding the transmission time of the target virtual link V L i since it does not effectively take into consideration the overlapping between blocking time and transmission time in the transmission processes of adjacent hops. The relationship between the transmission time of V L i and the inference I k i across any arbitrary hop k can certainly affect the pessimism of the estimation.
At the k th hop, we define µ k as.
div.formula: µ k ≜ w k i -C i(7)
div.p: µ k represents the amount of blocking time consumed by all frames transmitted before the target frame V L i . µ k is numerically the same as the inference I k i . However, its transmission timestamp takes place less pessimistically than the inference I k i does. This difference is crucial to analyzing limitation of RTA, which is fully explained by the rest of this section.

In any transmission hop k, the transmission of the target virtual link V L i starts if and only if both the blocking amount µ k and transmission process C i of the frame from target V L i have already been completed. This brings the potential overlapping between the transmission of the target frames and the transmission of the blocking amount in the next hop, which leads to an overestimation of the worst-case delay w k i of the current hop and accumulates the pessimism of the final worstcase delay W i .

In all three cases of the 2-hop transmission process, the WCD produced by RTA introduces pessimism of a constant amount of C i or I i depending on network architecture configurations, where the overestimation accumulates as the end-to-end transmission of the target VL proceeds with the increment of hop number.

div.head: C. Blocking-Waived Estimation (BWE)
div.p: Recognizing the inherent pessimism in RTA calculations as discussed above, and also inspired by the work in tightening the WCD [25], we introduce BWE, a novel approach aimed at mitigating this pessimism in WCD computation. BWE achieves this by meticulously analyzing the intricate relationship between the blocking time at each hop and the transmission time of the target frame. Importantly, this methodology can be generalized to n-hop scenarios.

In the context of BWE, the initiation of transmission in the (k +1) th hop commences only after the end of blocking in the k th hop. Moreover, the transmission of the target frame at the (k + 1) th hop is contingent upon the simultaneous completion of both the k th -hop transmission of the target frame and the blocking at the (k + 1) th hop. This synchronization ensures a more accurate and less pessimistic estimation of WCD, addressing the limitations observed in traditional RTA computations.

The fundamental concept underlying BWE is illustrated in Algorithm 2 and involves an analysis of the correlation between the transmission time of frames from a target VL and the blocking amounts encountered across different transmission hops. The algorithm recursively computes the blocking time in each hop, as in RTA, and stores these blocking times in a set denoted as δ (Line 12). Subsequently, in the final step of the computation, the method Blocking_Analysis is invoked (Line 13). This method accumulates the blocking time in δ from the first hop to the final hop (Line 21) and appends the result to a list β (Line 22).

Within a for loop starting from Line 23 to 27, we compute the end-to-end WCD as follows: for the first hop, transmission time of target VL C i and blocking time at the first hop are added to W i (Line 25); for hops beyond it, we take the maximum of WCD from the preceding hop and accumulated blocking time up to the current hop (Line 27).

div.p: Notably, regardless of the scale of the transmission process, BWE ensures a reduction in pessimism in the end-to-end WCD, owing to its intrinsic capability to alleviate the original overlapping computation inherent in RTA.

In general, the end-to-end WCD is thus computed based on the analysis of the relationship between the transmission time of frames from a target V L i and the blocking time across all transmission hops. It ultimately yields a theoretical WCD estimate that is more stringent than what RTA provides, as shown by the figures 1-3. We also believe that the complexity of BWE is similar to RTA as BWE reduces the pessimism by calling the analysis function on Line 13, which intrinsically has an extra computational complexity linear to the number of hops. Since RTA naturally traverses every hop for each target VL, the additional computation of BWE does not elevate the computational complexity to a higher level.

div.head: V. COMPARISON OF THE APPROACHES
div.p: In this section, we consider a representative AFDX usecase network architecture with two switches [2]. For this network, we calculate WCD upper bounds using response-time analysis (RTA), compositional performance analysis (CPA), and network calculus (NC), complemented by WCD lower bounds via discrete-event simulation. NC results are obtained by using the Saihu framework [4], while results of CPA are implemented by pyCPA. RTA and BWE implementations adhere to Algorithm 1 and 2, respectively.

div.head: A. Network Description
div.p: As above-mentioned, for making numerical comparisons, we choose to consider the dual-switch AFDX (avionics fullduplex Ethernet) network architecture described in [2] and illustrated in Figure 6. The architecture comprises 4 endsystems (ES) and 13 virtual links (VLs), as detailed in Table WCD. We obtained simulated outputs for all VLs using Java Modeling tools depicted as strict lower bound for all WCD approaches in the following figures. Note that there are only three simulated VLs reported in [2]. The Sim. values aim to strengthen the correctness of WCD computations as outputs of all other approaches should appear to be higher than the Sim. ones.

We have carried out a series of comparative experiments on Figure 6 with BWE, CPA, RTA, and NC: From Table III, we can observe that CPA and RTA provide exactly the same result for all virtual links within the architecture. Results from BWE and NC share all the tightest WCDs of virtual links within the network. In particular, BWE provides the tightest worst-case delay results for eight virtual links (V L {1,4,5,6,9,10,11,13} ) out of thirteen, which composes of more than half of all virtual links within the architecture Figure 6.

The last two row of Table III contain total ( 13 i=1 W CD i ) and average ( 13i=1 W CD i /13) delay bounds of all virtual links for all methods. The summation and average delay bounds provide a cumulative assessment of WCD across all evaluated VLs, offering a more comprehensive overview of the overall performance of each method. Upon examining the average WCD bounds, it becomes evident that BWE presents an average WCD bound of 450µs, which is significantly lower than those observed for CPA and RTA (both at 518µs), and NC (475µs).

Moreover, as BWE aims to reduce the pessimism of RTA, the Rel. (Relative) Reductions specifically between results from RTA and BWE is computed in Table III. Notably, across all VLs, BWE outperforms both CPA and RTA without exception. From V L 1 to V L 13 , the relative reductions between worst-case delays calculated by RTA and BWE range from 2.63% in V L 8 to 34.34% in V L 11 , with an overall reduction rate of 13.14%, as shown in Table III, which shows a significant reduction of the pessimism in the estimation.

Table III provides all the results. In what follows, we further discuss the performance improvement of BWE by comparing with RTA/CPA and NC respectively. We choose to visually show the differences on WCD values of VLs in terms of curves (Figures 7 and8), although there is no direct relationship between VLs. III. Firstly, we can notice that BWE and RTA/CPA always remain greater than the simulation results for each VL. This is expected because the simulation provides lower bounds for the WCD. It also verifies that RTA and CPA do not suffer from the optimistic issue. Secondly, we observe that BWE consistently outperforms RTA/CPA in terms of reducing pessimism.

div.head: Fig. 8: Comparison between delay bounds obtained by BWE and NC on different VLs
div.p: Due to the fact that RTA/CPA and BWE are both categorized in the class of real-time scheduling theory, it is necessary to carry out a comparison with NC-based approaches for comprehensive validation. Saihu [4] has been used that allowed us to obtain several results presenting more or less pessimism. We chose here the tightest one that has been produced by adapting Panco tool2 [26] from FIFO to Fixed-Priority FIFO. Keeping this in mind, the WCD values calculated by BWE and NC using Panco tool are plotted in Figure 8. On the one hand, holding a similar changing trend across all curves of VLs, neither BWE nor NC has any values that are lower than the simulation one (i.e. no optimistic issue). On the other hand, unlike the previous comparison, where BWE outperforms RTA/CPA for all VLs, this figure shows that BWE is not always more advantageous in reducing WCD pessimism than NC. As can be seen for V L 3,9,11 , BWE reaches largely lower values than NC, but for several VLs, e.g., V L 2,12 , NC's delay bounds are less pessimistic.

div.head: VI. CONCLUSION
div.p: This paper delves into an investigation concerning different Worst-Case Delay (WCD) analysis approaches regarding overestimation, i.e., pessimism. Having the purpose of reducing such pessimism, particularly addressing the limitations in RTA, we propose BWE, a recursive algorithm designed to analyze the intricate relationship between the transmission time of the target frame and the blocking time across the various hops of the transmission.

The numerical results on a use-case demonstrate that BWE yields more stringent WCD bounds for all VLs in comparison to RTA/CPA and, to a partial extent, NC. The observed relative and absolute reductions amount to 34.34% and 242µs, respectively. Beyond its efficacy in reducing pessimism in WCD calculation when compared to other approaches, such as RTA/CPA and NC in the exemplified network, BWE is also extended to n-hop scenarios. In addition to approaches belonging to a single class, there are also researchers who explore connections between NC and RTA and strive to combine both, some of which have demonstrated reasonable improvements in WCD calculation [23,27]. The potential direction of studying BWE can be to investigate nuanced differences between BWE and other approaches [23][27] and to better understand the reason behind the performance of BWE, like in Figure 8.

BWE can also be generalized to cases where a network architecture has different transmission rates. The end-to-end WCD is calculated in a similar manner but with fixed transmission time in the original computation, replaced with an array of transmission time in each hop. These extensions and generalizations demonstrate potential of BWE in providing tighter WCD estimates for a broader range of network architectures. Finally, extending BWE to study the WCD of data flows in TSN under credit-based shaper is one of our ongoing work.
